title: Leetcodify Friends Recommendations
statement:
A music app logs what people play and who is friends with whom:

- `Listens(user_id, song_id, day)`: user `user_id` played song `song_id` on date `day`. The table has no key, so the same play can be logged more than once.
- `Friendship(user1_id, user2_id)`: `user1_id` and `user2_id` are friends (in both directions). Each pair is stored once, with `user1_id < user2_id`.

The app recommends user `y` to user `x` when both hold:

- `x` and `y` are different people and are not friends;
- on some **single** day, `x` and `y` both played at least **three different** songs in common.

A recommendation has a direction: when `x` and `y` qualify, report both `(x, y)` and `(y, x)`. Report each recommendation once, even if the pair qualifies on several days. Output columns: `user_id` (who receives the recommendation) and `recommended_id`. Rows may come in any order.
constraints: Listens has no primary key and may contain duplicate rows
user1_id < user2_id in every Friendship row
reference:
WITH friends AS (
  SELECT user1_id AS user_id, user2_id AS friend_id
  FROM Friendship
  UNION ALL
  SELECT user2_id, user1_id
  FROM Friendship
),
song_matches AS (
  SELECT a.user_id, b.user_id AS recommended_id, a.day
  FROM Listens AS a
  JOIN Listens AS b
    ON b.day = a.day
   AND b.song_id = a.song_id
   AND b.user_id <> a.user_id
  GROUP BY a.user_id, b.user_id, a.day
  HAVING COUNT(DISTINCT a.song_id) >= 3
)
SELECT DISTINCT m.user_id, m.recommended_id
FROM song_matches AS m
LEFT JOIN friends AS f
  ON f.user_id = m.user_id
 AND f.friend_id = m.recommended_id
WHERE f.user_id IS NULL;
brute:
WITH plays AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id, song_id, day
  FROM Listens
)
SELECT DISTINCT c.user_id, c.recommended_id
FROM (
  SELECT p.user_id, q.user_id AS recommended_id
  FROM plays AS p
  JOIN plays AS q ON q.day = p.day AND q.song_id = p.song_id AND q.user_id <> p.user_id
  GROUP BY p.user_id, q.user_id, p.day
  HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3
) AS c
WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Friendship AS f WHERE f.user1_id = c.user_id AND f.user2_id = c.recommended_id)
  AND NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM Friendship AS f WHERE f.user1_id = c.recommended_id AND f.user2_id = c.user_id)
notes:
## Intuition

Two people "match" on a day when the songs they both played that day number at least three. Pairs of plays of the same song on the same day by different users are exactly what a self-join of `Listens` produces, so grouping that self-join by (user, other user, day) and counting **distinct** songs finds every match. What remains is to drop pairs who are already friends, an anti-join against a friendship list made symmetric, and to remove repeats from pairs that match on several days.

## Approach

1. `friends`: each `Friendship` row in both directions, since the table stores each pair once with the smaller id first.
2. `song_matches`: self-join `Listens` as `a` and `b` on the same `day` and `song_id` with different users, group by `a.user_id`, `b.user_id` and `day`, and keep groups with `COUNT(DISTINCT a.song_id) >= 3`.
3. Left join `friends` on the ordered pair and keep rows where no friendship was found.
4. `SELECT DISTINCT` the pair, so a pair that matches on two days appears once.

## Example 1, step by step

- On 2021-03-15, users 1, 2 and 3 all played songs 10, 11 and 12, while user 4 played 10, 11 and 13. User 5 played 10, 11 and 12, but on 2021-03-16, when nobody else listened.
- `song_matches` holds the six ordered pairs among users 1, 2 and 3 (three common songs each). User 4 shares only two songs with each of them, and user 5 shares a day with nobody.
- `friends` holds `(1, 2)` and `(2, 1)`, so the anti-join removes those two rows.
- The answer is `(1, 3)`, `(2, 3)`, `(3, 1)` and `(3, 2)`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(L + P) with hashing, where L is the number of listens and P the self-join size, the sum over (day, song) of the squared number of plays; the friendship anti-join adds O(F).
- Space: O(P) for the joined rows before grouping.

## Pitfalls

- Duplicate plays inflate `COUNT(*)` (two copies on each side become four joined rows); count `DISTINCT` songs.
- The day belongs both in the join and in the grouping. Without it in the join, songs played on different days match; without it in the grouping, two shared songs on one day plus one on another add up to three.
- `Friendship` keeps only `user1_id < user2_id`; checking one direction recommends friends to each other.
- Without `DISTINCT`, a pair that matches on several days is reported several times.

## Clauses

| Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- |
| `friends` | every friendship as (`user_id`, `friend_id`) in both directions |
| `a`, `b` | two plays of the same song on the same day by different users |
| `song_matches` / `m` | (user, other user, day) with at least three common songs |
| `f` | the friendship row for the pair, null when they are not friends |

narration.1: The first stage lists every friendship in both directions.
narration.4: UNION ALL appends each pair reversed, since Friendship stores it once with the smaller id first.
narration.8: The second stage finds pairs of users who share enough songs on one day.
narration.11: Joining Listens to itself pairs up plays of the same song on the same day by two different users.
narration.15: Each group is one ordered pair of users on one day.
narration.16: Counting distinct songs ignores repeated plays; three or more common songs makes a match.
narration.18: DISTINCT reports a pair once even when it matches on several days.
narration.20: A left join looks for a friendship between the two users.
narration.23: Keeping only rows with no friendship found removes people who are already friends.
